title: AP Human Geography: Terms

sources.name: Original educational synthesis from general knowledge

description: For AP Human Geography students reviewing spatial thinking, population, culture, politics, agriculture, development and cities through original definitions and short examples.

cards.back: Study of how people organize space, interact with environments, and create places.
cards.example: Studying migration between cities is human geography.

cards.back: Study of Earth's natural features and processes.
cards.example: Studying river erosion is physical geography.

cards.back: A position specified by a fixed reference system.
cards.example: Latitude and longitude identify an absolute location.

cards.back: A position described in relation to other places.
cards.example: A town lies upstream from a port.

cards.back: Angular distance north or south of the equator.
cards.example: The equator is at zero degrees latitude.

cards.back: Angular distance east or west of the prime meridian.
cards.example: A location can be 30 degrees east longitude.

cards.back: The zero-degree latitude line dividing northern and southern hemispheres.
cards.example: Places on the equator have zero latitude.

cards.back: The conventional zero-degree longitude reference passing through Greenwich.
cards.example: Longitude is measured east or west from it.

cards.back: The physical and human characteristics at a settlement's actual location.
cards.example: A harbor's sheltered bay is a site advantage.

cards.back: A location's position relative to surrounding places and connections.
cards.example: A town at a trade-route crossing has a useful situation.

cards.back: A location with distinctive physical and human characteristics.
cards.example: A neighborhood has architecture and local traditions.

cards.back: Meanings and attachments associated with a particular location.
cards.example: Residents identify strongly with a historic market.

cards.back: The geographic extent within which phenomena are arranged.
cards.example: A geographer compares the spacing of settlements.

cards.back: The arrangement of a phenomenon across Earth's surface.
cards.example: Stores may cluster near a transit station.

cards.back: The amount of something per unit area.
cards.example: Population density can be people per square kilometer.

cards.back: How closely together or widely dispersed features are.
cards.example: Shops concentrated downtown occupy a small area.

cards.back: A recognizable arrangement of geographic features.
cards.example: Houses may form a linear pattern along a road.

cards.back: Features located close together rather than spread evenly.
cards.example: Restaurants gather around a plaza.

cards.back: Features spread relatively far apart.
cards.example: Farmhouses are scattered across fields.

cards.back: Features arranged along a line or corridor.
cards.example: Settlements follow a river.

cards.back: An area sharing one or more measurable or officially defined traits.
cards.example: A country is a formal political region.

cards.back: An area organized around a node and its interactions.
cards.example: A commuting region centers on a city.

cards.back: An area defined by people's ideas or feelings about it.
cards.example: People may disagree about the limits of the Midwest.

cards.back: Dividing space into regions using selected criteria.
cards.example: An analyst groups districts by climate and farming.

cards.back: The geographic level at which data are examined.
cards.example: A pattern may differ at national and neighborhood scales.

cards.back: The relationship between map distance and ground distance.
cards.example: One centimeter may represent one kilometer.

cards.back: A map showing a small area with relatively high detail.
cards.example: A neighborhood street map is large-scale.

cards.back: A map showing a large area with relatively low detail.
cards.example: A world map is small-scale.

cards.back: The design and production of maps.
cards.example: A cartographer selects symbols and projection.

cards.back: A method of representing Earth's curved surface on a flat surface.
cards.example: A projection trades off different kinds of distortion.

cards.back: A conformal cylindrical projection that preserves local angles while enlarging high-latitude areas.
cards.example: Greenland appears disproportionately large.

cards.back: A projection preserving relative areas while distorting some shapes or angles.
cards.example: It supports area comparisons between continents.

cards.back: A map primarily showing where features are located.
cards.example: A road atlas is a reference map.

cards.back: A map emphasizing a particular topic or variable.
cards.example: A map may show regional literacy levels.

cards.back: A map shading areas according to a variable, usually a rate or ratio.
cards.example: Counties are shaded by population density.

cards.back: A map using dots to represent quantities within areas.
cards.example: Each dot can represent a thousand residents.

cards.back: A map using symbol sizes to represent quantities.
cards.example: Larger circles indicate larger city populations.

cards.back: A map connecting places with equal values.
cards.example: Contour lines connect equal elevations.

cards.back: A map that resizes areas according to a statistical variable.
cards.example: Countries expand or shrink according to population.

cards.back: Geographic information systems: tools for storing, combining, analyzing, and displaying spatial data.
cards.example: Analysts overlay flood zones and housing locations.

cards.back: Global Positioning System: satellite-based positioning and timing technology.
cards.example: A receiver estimates its location from satellite signals.

cards.back: Collecting information about Earth's surface from a distance.
cards.example: A satellite image reveals urban expansion.

cards.back: Descriptive information about experiences or characteristics of places.
cards.example: Interviews describe residents' neighborhood attachments.

cards.back: Numerical measurements of geographic phenomena.
cards.example: A census records population counts.

cards.back: A tendency for two phenomena to occur in related locations.
cards.example: Transit access and apartment density may be associated.

cards.back: Movement or connection between places.
cards.example: Commuting links suburbs to employment centers.

cards.back: A tendency for interaction to weaken as distance increases.
cards.example: People often shop more frequently near home.

cards.back: The time, cost, or effort that distance adds to movement.
cards.example: Shipping costs can discourage distant trade.

cards.back: Reduced perceived distance because transport and communication become faster.
cards.example: Video calls connect distant offices instantly.

cards.back: The degree to which places are linked through networks.
cards.example: A hub airport increases a city's connectivity.

cards.back: The ease of reaching a place, service, or opportunity.
cards.example: A bus route improves access to a clinic.

cards.back: A model predicting stronger interaction between larger places and weaker interaction with greater distance.
cards.example: Two large nearby cities may exchange many commuters.

cards.back: Increasing connections and interdependence across the world.
cards.example: A product's parts come from several countries.

cards.back: The spread of an idea, trait, or practice across space.
cards.example: A new farming method spreads between villages.

cards.back: Spread through the movement of people carrying a trait.
cards.example: Migrants bring a language to a new region.

cards.back: Spread outward while a trait remains strong near its origin.
cards.example: A popular practice gains users in adjacent areas.

cards.back: Spread through widespread person-to-person contact or proximity.
cards.example: A local dance spreads among neighboring communities.

cards.back: Spread through ranked nodes or influential groups.
cards.example: A style spreads from major cities to smaller towns.

cards.back: Spread of an underlying idea that is adapted locally.
cards.example: A restaurant concept is modified for local diets.

cards.back: The visible imprint of human activity and values on the environment.
cards.example: Terraces, shrines, and roads shape a landscape.

cards.back: The discredited claim that physical environments rigidly determine cultures and social outcomes.
cards.example: It wrongly treats climate as destiny.

cards.back: The view that environments constrain possibilities while people make choices using culture and technology.
cards.example: Irrigation expands farming options in a dry area.

cards.back: Meeting present needs while maintaining environmental and social capacities for the future.
cards.example: Water use is limited to protect future supplies.

cards.back: The statistical study of human populations.
cards.example: Demographers analyze fertility and migration.

cards.back: Where people live across space.
cards.example: Many people live near coasts and river valleys.

cards.back: Total population divided by total land area.
cards.example: A region with 1,000 people in 10 square kilometers has density 100.

cards.back: Total population divided by arable land area.
cards.example: Limited farmland can produce high physiological density.

cards.back: Number of farmers divided by arable land area.
cards.example: Mechanized regions often have fewer farmers per unit of arable land.

cards.back: The population an environment can support under specified technology and consumption conditions.
cards.example: Irrigation may change a region's carrying capacity.

cards.back: The portion of Earth permanently inhabited by people.
cards.example: Permanent settlements form part of the ecumene.

cards.back: Annual live births per 1,000 people.
cards.example: A rate of 20 means 20 births per thousand residents per year.

cards.back: Annual deaths per 1,000 people.
cards.example: An older population may have a relatively high crude death rate.

cards.back: Births minus deaths, excluding migration.
cards.example: A population gains people naturally when births exceed deaths.

cards.back: Natural population change expressed as a percentage over a period.
cards.example: With crude rates per thousand, divide birth rate minus death rate by 10.

cards.back: The average number of children a woman would have under current age-specific fertility rates.
cards.example: A fertility decline can reduce future population growth.

cards.back: Fertility sufficient for a generation to replace itself without migration.
cards.example: It is about 2.1 in many low-mortality populations, but varies.

cards.back: Deaths before age one per 1,000 live births in a period.
cards.example: Improved sanitation can lower infant mortality.

cards.back: Expected years of life under prevailing age-specific mortality conditions.
cards.example: Life expectancy at birth summarizes mortality patterns.

cards.back: A graph showing population by age group and sex.
cards.example: A broad base often indicates many young children.

cards.back: The ratio of selected dependent-age groups to the working-age population.
cards.example: A common measure compares under-15 and 65-plus groups with ages 15–64.

cards.back: The burden represented by children relative to working-age people.
cards.example: A young population may need more schools.

cards.back: The relationship between older people and the working-age population.
cards.example: An aging population can increase demand for elder care.

cards.back: Continued growth after fertility falls because many people are entering reproductive ages.
cards.example: A youthful age structure can sustain births despite smaller families.

cards.back: The estimated time required for a population to double at a given growth rate.
cards.example: The rule of 70 gives about 35 years at 2% annual growth.

cards.back: A model of changes in birth and death rates associated with broad economic and social changes.
cards.example: Death rates typically fall before birth rates in the model.

cards.back: A model stage with high, fluctuating birth and death rates and low long-run growth.
cards.example: Population growth is limited by high mortality.

cards.back: A model stage with falling death rates and still-high birth rates.
cards.example: Population grows rapidly as mortality falls.

cards.back: A model stage in which birth rates decline and growth slows.
cards.example: Smaller desired families reduce fertility.

cards.back: A model stage with low birth and death rates and slow natural growth.
cards.example: Births and deaths may be near balance.

cards.back: A proposed extension with sustained very low fertility and possible natural decrease.
cards.example: Deaths may outnumber births in an aging population.

cards.back: A shift in dominant causes of illness and death as social and health conditions change.
cards.example: Chronic diseases become more prominent as infectious mortality declines.

cards.back: The argument that population can grow faster than food supply, creating pressure on resources.
cards.example: Malthus anticipated checks such as famine.

cards.back: A view emphasizing modern population and consumption pressure on finite resources.
cards.example: Analysts may connect growth to water scarcity.

cards.back: The idea that population pressure can stimulate agricultural innovation and intensification.
cards.example: Farmers intensify cultivation as land becomes scarce.

cards.back: A policy encouraging births.
cards.example: A government offers parental benefits to support childbearing.

cards.back: A policy intended to reduce fertility.
cards.example: A government expands voluntary family-planning access.

cards.back: A change of residence across a meaningful geographic boundary.
cards.example: A family moves from one country to another.

cards.back: Migration out of a place.
cards.example: Leaving one's origin country is emigration.

cards.back: Migration into a place.
cards.example: Entering a destination country to settle is immigration.

cards.back: Immigrants minus emigrants for a place and period.
cards.example: More arrivals than departures produce positive net migration.

cards.back: Movement of residence within a country.
cards.example: A worker moves from a village to a city.

cards.back: Movement of residence across national borders.
cards.example: A student settles in another country.

cards.back: Migration between regions within a larger territory.
cards.example: A household moves from the interior to the coast.

cards.back: Migration within the same region.
cards.example: A family moves from a city center to a nearby suburb.

cards.back: Movement in which migrants have substantial choice.
cards.example: A worker chooses a city with better employment.

cards.back: Movement caused by coercion, persecution, conflict, or severe threats.
cards.example: War forces residents to flee.

cards.back: A condition encouraging people to leave an origin.
cards.example: Lack of work can push migration.

cards.back: A condition attracting people to a destination.
cards.example: Educational opportunities can pull migrants.

cards.back: A barrier that limits migration or movement.
cards.example: A border restriction can interrupt a migration route.

cards.back: A closer opportunity that changes an intended destination.
cards.example: A migrant finds work before reaching the planned city.

cards.back: Migration facilitated by earlier migrants' social ties and assistance.
cards.example: Relatives help newcomers find housing.

cards.back: Migration through a sequence of intermediate destinations.
cards.example: A person moves from village to town to metropolis.

cards.back: Historical generalizations about migration patterns, including frequent short-distance moves and economic motives.
cards.example: They describe tendencies, not universal laws.

cards.back: A person outside their country who meets applicable protection criteria for persecution-related flight.
cards.example: Protection status depends on governing definitions and facts.

cards.back: Someone forced to leave home who remains within their country's borders.
cards.example: A displaced family moves to another province.

cards.back: A person seeking international protection whose claim has not yet been finally decided.
cards.example: A new applicant awaits a protection decision.

cards.back: Money or resources migrants send to people elsewhere, often at home.
cards.example: A worker sends earnings to family abroad.

cards.back: Loss of skilled people through emigration.
cards.example: A region loses many trained engineers.

cards.back: A migrant admitted to work under a host country's employment arrangement, often temporarily.
cards.example: A seasonal worker harvests crops abroad.

cards.back: Migration involving sustained social or economic ties across national borders.
cards.example: A household maintains businesses in two countries.

cards.back: Shared learned practices, beliefs, knowledge, and meanings.
cards.example: Food traditions and language are cultural features.

cards.back: A single element of culture.
cards.example: A greeting custom is a cultural trait.

cards.back: A related set of cultural traits.
cards.example: A holiday includes foods, rituals, and clothing.

cards.back: A place from which a cultural practice or innovation originates and spreads.
cards.example: An early agricultural region can be a hearth.

cards.back: Traditions associated with relatively small communities and local continuity.
cards.example: A locally transmitted craft is a folk practice.

cards.back: Widely circulated cultural practices associated with mass communication and broad audiences.
cards.example: A streamed song gains an international audience.

cards.back: Tangible objects and built forms associated with a culture.
cards.example: Tools and houses are material culture.

cards.back: Intangible beliefs, values, language, and norms.
cards.example: Ideas about hospitality are nonmaterial culture.

cards.back: Adopting some traits of another culture while retaining parts of one's own.
cards.example: A migrant learns a new language and keeps home traditions.

cards.back: A process in which a group becomes less culturally distinct within a dominant society.
cards.example: Later generations may adopt dominant language practices.

cards.back: Blending elements from different cultural traditions into new forms.
cards.example: A celebration combines several religious traditions.

cards.back: Coexistence and recognition of multiple cultural traditions within a society.
cards.example: Public institutions accommodate several community languages.

cards.back: Increasing similarity among cultures.
cards.example: Global media can spread shared fashions.

cards.back: Increasing difference or deliberate maintenance of cultural distinctions.
cards.example: A community revives a threatened language.

cards.back: Judging other cultures by one's own cultural standards.
cards.example: A traveler assumes unfamiliar customs are inferior.

cards.back: Understanding a practice in its cultural context.
cards.example: A researcher studies a ritual's local meaning.

cards.back: A broad group of languages descended from a common ancestral language.
cards.example: Indo-European is a language family.

cards.back: A major subdivision within a language family.
cards.example: Romance languages form a branch of Indo-European.

cards.back: A language variety with distinctive vocabulary, grammar, or pronunciation.
cards.example: A regional dialect may use local words.

cards.back: A boundary marking the geographic extent of a language feature.
cards.example: A map separates two pronunciations of a word.

cards.back: A shared language used by speakers of different native languages.
cards.example: Traders use a common language at a port.

cards.back: A contact language with limited initial functions and no native speakers at its emergence.
cards.example: Trade contact may produce a simplified shared language.

cards.back: A fully developed language arising from contact, often through a pidgin becoming a community's native language.
cards.example: Children may acquire a contact language as their first language.

cards.back: A language designated for governmental or legal functions.
cards.example: Government documents use an official language.

cards.back: A place name.
cards.example: A town's name may reflect a historical language.

cards.back: A religion generally seeking adherents across ethnic and geographic boundaries.
cards.example: Christianity and Islam are commonly classified this way.

cards.back: A religion closely associated with a particular people or place and usually less focused on universal conversion.
cards.example: Hinduism is commonly discussed in this category.

cards.back: Belief in one deity.
cards.example: Judaism is monotheistic.

cards.back: Belief in multiple deities.
cards.example: Many ancient Greek religious practices were polytheistic.

cards.back: A journey to a place of religious significance.
cards.example: A worshipper travels to a sacred site.

cards.back: A place with religious meaning for a community.
cards.example: A shrine can be a sacred site.

cards.back: Declining religious influence in aspects of social or institutional life.
cards.example: Civil institutions may become less tied to religious authority.

cards.back: Shared identity associated with ancestry, history, culture, or related ties.
cards.example: An ethnic community preserves shared traditions.

cards.back: A group with a shared identity and often a claim to political self-determination.
cards.example: A nation need not have its own sovereign state.

cards.back: A political entity with territory, population, government, and sovereignty.
cards.example: A sovereign country is a state in political geography.

cards.back: A state whose territorial and political identity largely aligns with one nation.
cards.example: It is an ideal type; real populations are often diverse.

cards.back: A state containing multiple national groups.
cards.example: Several nations may share one government.

cards.back: A nation lacking an independent sovereign state of its own.
cards.example: A national group may live across several countries.

cards.back: A nation spread across more than one state.
cards.example: A shared national identity can cross borders.

cards.back: Supreme political authority over a territory, subject to real-world constraints.
cards.example: A state makes laws within its territory.

cards.back: The principle that peoples should have a voice in their political status.
cards.example: A group seeks autonomy through a referendum.

cards.back: Efforts to control or influence people and resources by controlling space.
cards.example: A government regulates access across a border.

cards.back: Control of a territory and its people by an external power.
cards.example: An empire administers an overseas colony.

cards.back: Expansion of political, economic, or military dominance over other peoples or territories.
cards.example: A powerful state controls weaker regions indirectly.

cards.back: The process of ending colonial rule.
cards.example: A colony gains independence.

cards.back: Continuing external domination through economic or political influence after formal colonialism.
cards.example: Debt dependence can constrain a former colony's choices.

cards.back: A line or zone separating political or administrative territories.
cards.example: An international border separates states.

cards.back: A boundary drawn using straight lines or arcs rather than local cultural patterns.
cards.example: A border follows a line of latitude.

cards.back: A political boundary using a natural feature as a reference.
cards.example: A river marks part of a border.

cards.back: A boundary established before the cultural landscape it later divides develops.
cards.example: A border precedes dense settlement.

cards.back: A boundary drawn after a cultural landscape develops, often reflecting it.
cards.example: A border follows an established language divide.

cards.back: A boundary imposed without close regard for existing cultural patterns.
cards.example: An external power divides an ethnic region.

cards.back: A former political boundary still visible in the landscape or social patterns.
cards.example: Old fortifications mark a vanished border.

cards.back: Physically marking a boundary on the ground.
cards.example: Posts identify a surveyed border.

cards.back: Legally describing or mapping the precise course of a boundary.
cards.example: A treaty specifies coordinates.

cards.back: A force that strengthens cohesion within a state.
cards.example: Shared institutions can support unity.

cards.back: A force that weakens cohesion within a state.
cards.example: Severe regional inequality may deepen division.

cards.back: Transfer of authority from a central government to regional governments.
cards.example: A region gains control over education policy.

cards.back: A state constitutionally dividing powers between national and subnational governments.
cards.example: States or provinces hold protected governing powers.

cards.back: A state where ultimate authority is concentrated in the central government.
cards.example: Regional powers are largely granted by the center.

cards.back: Cooperation in which states share or delegate some authority to a larger organization.
cards.example: Members jointly regulate parts of a common market.

cards.back: Fragmentation of a larger political unit into smaller, often antagonistic units.
cards.example: A state breaks into rival successor states.

cards.back: A claim to territory in another state based on national or historical ties.
cards.example: A government seeks land inhabited by its ethnic kin.

cards.back: Manipulating electoral district boundaries to favor a political interest.
cards.example: District lines concentrate opponents in a few seats.

cards.back: Redistribution of legislative seats among geographic units, often after a census.
cards.example: Population shifts alter states' seat totals.

cards.back: Redrawing electoral district boundaries.
cards.example: A legislature adjusts district lines after population change.

cards.back: Cultivation of crops and raising of animals for human use.
cards.example: Farmers grow grain and raise cattle.

cards.back: Selective adaptation of plants or animals to human use over generations.
cards.example: Breeding changes a crop's useful traits.

cards.back: Farming primarily to feed the farmer's household or local community.
cards.example: A family grows most of its own staple food.

cards.back: Farming primarily to sell products in markets.
cards.example: A farm sells grain to a processor.

cards.back: Farming with high labor or capital input per unit of land.
cards.example: Market gardening can use intensive inputs.

cards.back: Farming using relatively large land areas with lower inputs per unit area.
cards.example: Ranching may occupy broad grasslands.

cards.back: A system of cultivating plots temporarily and later leaving them fallow while using other land.
cards.example: Farmers rotate use among forest clearings.

cards.back: Clearing vegetation by cutting and burning before cultivation.
cards.example: Ash temporarily adds nutrients to a cleared plot.

cards.back: Herding with regular movement in search of grazing and water.
cards.example: Herders move livestock among seasonal pastures.

cards.back: Seasonal movement of livestock between pastures, often at different elevations.
cards.example: Herds move uphill in summer.

cards.back: Large-scale production of commercial crops, often historically linked to colonial labor systems.
cards.example: An estate grows tea for sale.

cards.back: A system combining crop cultivation with animal raising.
cards.example: Crops feed animals and manure fertilizes fields.

cards.back: Intensive production of vegetables, fruits, or flowers for sale.
cards.example: A farm supplies fresh produce to nearby cities.

cards.back: Farming adapted to dry summers and mild wetter winters.
cards.example: Olives and grapes are common crops.

cards.back: Cultivation of one crop across an area or repeated cycle.
cards.example: A large field grows only corn.

cards.back: Changing crops grown on a field across seasons or years.
cards.example: Legumes alternate with grain.

cards.back: Harvesting two crops from the same land within a year.
cards.example: A warm region grows rice followed by another crop.

cards.back: Land temporarily left uncropped to recover or manage moisture and nutrients.
cards.example: A field rests for a season.

cards.back: Artificial application of water to crops.
cards.example: Canals supply water to dry fields.

cards.back: Creating stepped fields on slopes.
cards.example: Terraces reduce runoff on a hillside.

cards.back: Twentieth-century spread of high-yield crop varieties with irrigation and chemical inputs.
cards.example: Wheat yields rose with new varieties and fertilizers.

cards.back: Commercial activities linking farm production to inputs, processing, distribution, and sales.
cards.example: A company supplies seeds and buys harvests.

cards.back: Linked stages through which a product is produced and distributed.
cards.example: Coffee moves from farm to processor to retailer.

cards.back: A model relating agricultural land use to transport costs and land rent around a market.
cards.example: Perishable or costly-to-transport goods locate nearer the city in the model.

cards.back: The idea that land users compete for locations according to accessibility and expected returns.
cards.example: Central sites command high rents from users valuing access.

cards.back: Reliable access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food for an active healthy life.
cards.example: A household can obtain adequate food throughout the year.

cards.back: An area with limited practical access to affordable nutritious food, under a chosen definition.
cards.example: Residents may face long trips to a full-service grocer.

cards.back: Land degradation in drylands caused by climatic and human factors.
cards.example: Overgrazing can contribute to dryland degradation.

cards.back: Accumulation of salts in soil, often associated with irrigation and evaporation.
cards.example: Poor drainage leaves salts in a field.

cards.back: Removal of forest cover for other land uses.
cards.example: Forest is cleared for pasture.

cards.back: Expansion of machine-based manufacturing and associated economic changes.
cards.example: Factories employ a growing share of workers.

cards.back: Economic activities extracting or harvesting natural resources.
cards.example: Farming and mining belong to the primary sector.

cards.back: Economic activities processing materials and manufacturing goods.
cards.example: A factory assembles appliances.

cards.back: Economic activities providing services.
cards.example: Retail and transport are service activities.

cards.back: Knowledge and information-oriented economic activities.
cards.example: Research and data analysis are examples.

cards.back: High-level decision-making and leadership activities in a common sector classification.
cards.example: Senior public policy leadership is often classified here.

cards.back: The value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a period.
cards.example: Domestic factory output contributes to GDP.

cards.back: Income received by residents, including net primary income from abroad.
cards.example: Residents' foreign investment income can affect GNI.

cards.back: A conversion approach adjusting for differences in price levels.
cards.example: PPP comparisons consider what income can buy locally.

cards.back: A composite measure of health, education, and income dimensions.
cards.example: Life expectancy contributes to its health dimension.

cards.back: A measure of inequality in a distribution, commonly income.
cards.example: A higher value generally indicates greater inequality.

cards.back: A multidimensional process of change in economic opportunities and human well-being.
cards.example: Improved education can be part of development.

cards.back: A stage-based theory proposing a progression from traditional society to mass consumption.
cards.example: Its universal sequence is widely criticized.

cards.back: A framework interpreting global inequality through core, semiperipheral, and peripheral relationships.
cards.example: Production links regions with unequal bargaining power.

cards.back: In world-systems theory, a region with strong capital, institutions, and high-value activities.
cards.example: Core firms may control profitable production stages.

cards.back: In world-systems theory, regions often dependent on lower-value or extractive activities.
cards.example: A region exports raw materials to dominant markets.

cards.back: Regions with a mix of core and peripheral roles in the global economy.
cards.example: A country both assembles exports and controls regional firms.

cards.back: The view that unequal external relationships can reproduce underdevelopment.
cards.example: Raw-material dependence can limit local industrial growth.

cards.back: Benefits firms gain by locating near related firms, workers, and services.
cards.example: A technology cluster shares skilled labor.

cards.back: Falling average costs as production increases over a relevant range.
cards.example: A larger plant spreads fixed costs across more units.

cards.back: A model locating industry by transport, labor, and agglomeration costs.
cards.example: A heavy-input factory may locate near raw materials.

cards.back: An industry whose final product weighs or occupies less than its inputs.
cards.example: Ore processing removes waste near a mine.

cards.back: An industry whose product is heavier or bulkier than key shipped inputs.
cards.example: Bottling adds local water near customers.

cards.back: An industry with relatively weak dependence on specific raw-material or market locations.
cards.example: Some digital services can operate in many places.

cards.back: Contracting work to an external organization.
cards.example: A firm hires another company to handle support.

cards.back: Moving an activity to another country, whether inside or outside the firm.
cards.example: A company relocates assembly abroad.

cards.back: A designated area with distinct rules or incentives to attract economic activity.
cards.example: A zone offers simplified procedures for exporters.

cards.back: Decline in manufacturing employment or importance in an economy or area.
cards.example: A former factory district shifts toward services.

cards.back: Economic activity operating partly or wholly outside formal regulation or reporting.
cards.example: An unregistered vendor sells meals.

cards.back: Growth in the share of people living in urban areas.
cards.example: Migration and reclassification can raise the urban share.

cards.back: Growth of population and activity on the outskirts of cities.
cards.example: Households move to peripheral residential areas.

cards.back: Movement from larger urban areas toward smaller towns or rural places.
cards.example: Remote workers settle outside major metropolitan areas.

cards.back: The concentrated commercial and office core of a city.
cards.example: Tall office buildings cluster downtown.

cards.back: An ordering of settlements by size and functions.
cards.example: Metropolises provide services absent from small towns.

cards.back: A model explaining settlement spacing through markets for goods and services.
cards.example: Higher-order centers serve larger hinterlands.

cards.back: The minimum customer base needed to support a good or service.
cards.example: A specialist shop needs enough regular buyers.

cards.back: The maximum distance consumers are willing to travel for it in a model.
cards.example: People travel farther for rare specialist care than for bread.

cards.back: An idealized pattern where a city's population is inversely related to its rank.
cards.example: The second city would be about half the largest city's size.

cards.back: A city disproportionately dominant in population and influence within its urban system.
cards.example: One metropolis greatly exceeds the next largest city.

cards.back: An urban model with land uses arranged in rings around a central core.
cards.example: Residential zones extend outward from downtown in the model.

cards.back: An urban model in which land-use wedges extend along transport corridors.
cards.example: Industry follows a rail corridor outward.

cards.back: An urban model with several activity centers rather than a single dominant center.
cards.example: Airports and industrial districts form separate nodes.

cards.back: A substantial concentration of employment, shopping, and offices outside a traditional downtown.
cards.example: A highway interchange develops into a major business center.

cards.back: Low-density outward urban expansion, often separated by land use and car-oriented.
cards.example: New subdivisions spread beyond older built-up areas.

cards.back: Neighborhood reinvestment and socioeconomic change that may displace lower-income residents.
cards.example: Renovation and rising rents alter a central neighborhood.

cards.back: Discriminatory denial or restriction of financial services based on neighborhood classification.
cards.example: Mortgage access is restricted in a racialized area.

cards.back: Spatial separation of social groups in housing.
cards.example: Income groups occupy different neighborhoods.

cards.back: Housing developed outside some formal planning, tenure, or building systems.
cards.example: Residents build homes without secure title.

cards.back: Planning that promotes compact development, mixed uses, and efficient infrastructure.
cards.example: New housing is added near existing transit.

cards.back: A design movement favoring walkable neighborhoods, mixed uses, and connected streets.
cards.example: Homes and shops share a pedestrian-friendly district.

cards.back: Compact, mixed-use development focused around public transport.
cards.example: Apartments and shops cluster near a rail station.

cards.back: Higher temperatures in built-up areas than nearby less-developed areas.
cards.example: Pavement and limited vegetation raise local heat.

cards.back: Fair treatment and meaningful participation in environmental decisions and burdens.
cards.example: Residents seek equitable protection from industrial pollution.
